dbms-concurrency-recovery:0.prompt: Transaction T1 holds a shared (S) lock on row R. T2 then requests an S lock on R, and T3 requests an exclusive (X) lock on R. Under standard lock compatibility, what happens?
options: T2 and T3 both wait until T1 releases its lock
T2 is granted immediately; T3 waits
T3 is granted immediately because writers have priority; T2 waits
Both are granted because only one of them writes
dbms-concurrency-recovery:0.explanation: S locks are compatible with each other, so T2 is granted. X is incompatible with any other lock, so T3 must wait for all S holders to release. Writers do not pre-empt existing readers in a plain S/X scheme.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:0.prompt: What defines the two phases in two-phase locking (2PL)?
options: A read phase where data is copied, then a validation phase before writing
A prepare phase where participants vote, then a commit phase
A growing phase that only acquires locks, then a shrinking phase that only releases them
A phase that takes shared locks, then a phase that upgrades all of them to exclusive
dbms-concurrency-recovery:0.explanation: In 2PL a transaction may acquire locks until it releases its first lock; after that it may only release. The prepare/commit phases describe two-phase commit, a different protocol, and read/validate describes optimistic concurrency control.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:0.prompt: Basic (non-strict) 2PL guarantees conflict-serializable schedules. Which problem can it still produce?
options: Cascading aborts, because another transaction may read data written by a transaction that later aborts
Lost updates, because two writers can hold exclusive locks on the same row
Non-serializable schedules whenever more than two transactions run
Deadlock-free execution that starves readers
dbms-concurrency-recovery:0.explanation: Basic 2PL may release an X lock before commit, letting others read uncommitted data; if the writer aborts, readers must abort too (cascading aborts). Lost updates are prevented because X locks are exclusive.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:0.prompt: What distinguishes strict 2PL from rigorous (strong strict) 2PL?
options: Strict 2PL holds all locks until commit; rigorous 2PL releases shared locks early
Strict 2PL holds exclusive locks until commit or abort; rigorous 2PL holds all locks, shared and exclusive, until then
Strict 2PL forbids lock upgrades; rigorous 2PL allows them
Strict 2PL uses timestamps; rigorous 2PL uses a wait-for graph
dbms-concurrency-recovery:0.explanation: Strict 2PL keeps write (X) locks to the end, which makes schedules cascadeless. Rigorous 2PL keeps every lock to the end, so transactions serialize in commit order. The first option swaps the two definitions.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:0.prompt: Which lock sequence for a single transaction violates two-phase locking?
options: lock-S(A), lock-X(B), unlock(A), unlock(B)
lock-X(A), lock-X(B), unlock(B), unlock(A)
lock-S(A), lock-S(B), unlock(A), unlock(B)
lock-X(A), unlock(A), lock-X(B), unlock(B)
dbms-concurrency-recovery:0.explanation: After unlock(A) the transaction is in its shrinking phase, so acquiring lock-X(B) breaks 2PL. In the other sequences every acquire happens before the first release, and the release order doesn't matter.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:0.prompt: In PostgreSQL, transaction A runs SELECT ... FOR SHARE on a row. Which request from transaction B on the same row is blocked until A finishes?
options: Another SELECT ... FOR SHARE
A plain SELECT
An UPDATE of that row
A SELECT ... FOR KEY SHARE
dbms-concurrency-recovery:0.explanation: FOR SHARE blocks UPDATE, DELETE and FOR UPDATE / FOR NO KEY UPDATE on the row, but other FOR SHARE and FOR KEY SHARE lockers are compatible. Plain SELECTs never block on row locks thanks to MVCC.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:0.prompt: With multi-granularity locking, T1 holds an intention-exclusive (IX) lock on table orders because it is updating a few rows. T2 requests a shared (S) lock on the whole table. What happens?
options: T2 waits, because S on the table conflicts with IX
T2 is granted, because S and IX are both compatible with row locks
T2 is granted, but T1's row locks are upgraded to table locks
T1 is aborted to let T2 read a consistent table
dbms-concurrency-recovery:0.explanation: IX signals that some rows below are being written; a table-wide S lock would let T2 read those rows, so S and IX are incompatible. Intention locks exist so this conflict is detected at table level without scanning every row lock.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:0.prompt: Under 2PL with only row-level locks on existing rows, T1 runs SELECT COUNT(*) FROM seats WHERE flight=7 twice. T2 inserts a new seat for flight 7 and commits between the two counts. Why can T1 see different counts?
options: Shared locks are released after each statement under 2PL
The new row did not exist when T1 locked, so no lock blocked the insert: a phantom
COUNT(*) bypasses the lock manager
T2's insert upgraded T1's shared locks to exclusive
dbms-concurrency-recovery:0.explanation: Row locks only protect rows that exist. Stopping phantoms needs predicate, index-range or next-key locks covering 'flight=7'. 2PL doesn't release locks per statement, so the first option misdescribes it.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:0.prompt: Which pairs of lock modes are compatible (both can be held on the same object by different transactions)? Select all that apply.
options: S and S
IS and IX
S and X
IX and S
IX and IX
dbms-concurrency-recovery:0.explanation: S/S share reads; IS/IX and IX/IX only announce intentions on finer-grained items, so they are compatible at table level. S conflicts with X, and a table-level S conflicts with IX because the IX holder is writing rows below.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:0.prompt: A long-running transaction uses strict 2PL and updates many rows early on. Which consequences follow? Select all that apply.
options: Other transactions that want those rows wait until it commits or aborts
No other transaction can read its uncommitted writes, so aborts don't cascade
Deadlocks are still possible with other transactions
Lock contention drops, because all locks are released in one batch
Deadlocks become impossible, because locks are held to the end
dbms-concurrency-recovery:0.explanation: Holding X locks to the end makes schedules cascadeless, but rows stay blocked for longer, and deadlocks can still occur because lock acquisition order isn't controlled. Releasing locks in one batch at the end increases contention rather than reducing it.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:0.prompt: Two-phase locking guarantees that transactions can never deadlock.
options: True
False
dbms-concurrency-recovery:0.explanation: 2PL guarantees conflict-serializability, not deadlock freedom. T1 locking A then B while T2 locks B then A deadlocks under 2PL. You still need detection, timeouts or prevention schemes such as wait-die.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:1.prompt: Two API handlers run concurrently. Handler 1 updates account A then account B in one transaction; handler 2 updates B then A. They occasionally deadlock. What is the simplest application-level fix?
options: Raise the isolation level to SERIALIZABLE
Increase the connection pool size
Always lock or update the accounts in a consistent order, such as ascending id
Add a sleep between the two updates
dbms-concurrency-recovery:1.explanation: A consistent global lock order removes the circular wait, so this pair can't deadlock. SERIALIZABLE adds serialization failures and doesn't change lock ordering; a bigger pool or a sleep only changes timing.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:1.prompt: How does PostgreSQL resolve a deadlock between two transactions?
options: After waiting deadlock_timeout it checks for a cycle in the wait-for graph and aborts one transaction with a 'deadlock detected' error
It prevents deadlocks up front with wound-wait timestamps
It lets both wait until statement_timeout cancels them
It silently retries the later transaction
dbms-concurrency-recovery:1.explanation: PostgreSQL detects deadlocks rather than preventing them: once a lock wait exceeds deadlock_timeout (default 1s) it searches for a cycle and aborts a victim with SQLSTATE 40P01. The application must retry. It does not use timestamp schemes.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:1.prompt: Under the wait-die scheme, T5 (timestamp 5, older) requests a lock held by T9 (timestamp 9, younger). What happens?
options: T5 is aborted and restarted
T5 waits for T9
T9 is aborted so T5 can proceed
Both are aborted
dbms-concurrency-recovery:1.explanation: Wait-die: an older requester waits; a younger requester dies. So T5 waits. Aborting the younger holder (T9) is what wound-wait does.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:1.prompt: Under the wound-wait scheme, T5 (older) requests a lock held by T9 (younger). What happens?
options: T5 waits for T9
T5 is aborted and restarted with a new timestamp
T9 is wounded (aborted) and T5 gets the lock
The lock is shared between both
dbms-concurrency-recovery:1.explanation: Wound-wait: an older requester pre-empts (wounds) a younger holder; a younger requester waits. So T9 is rolled back. Older-waits is the wait-die rule.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:1.prompt: In wait-die and wound-wait, why does an aborted transaction restart with its ORIGINAL timestamp?
options: So it keeps getting older relative to new transactions and eventually wins, which prevents starvation
Because new timestamps would require a global clock
So the log manager can reuse its old log records
To make it lose every future conflict and keep the system fair
dbms-concurrency-recovery:1.explanation: Keeping the original timestamp means the restarted transaction becomes the oldest over time, and older transactions are never killed by younger ones in either scheme, so it eventually completes. A new timestamp could keep it young and starving forever.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:1.prompt: A DBMS builds a wait-for graph where an edge Ti → Tj means Ti waits for a lock held by Tj. When does a deadlock exist?
options: When any transaction has more than one outgoing edge
When the graph contains a cycle
When a node has no incoming edges
When the graph has more edges than nodes
dbms-concurrency-recovery:1.explanation: A cycle means every transaction in it waits for another one in it, so none can proceed. Multiple outgoing edges (waiting on several holders) or a high edge count are normal blocking, not deadlock.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:1.prompt: Several Node workers each run INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE for batches of 500 rows, in whatever order the rows arrive, against PostgreSQL. Under load they hit intermittent 'deadlock detected' (40P01) errors. What is the best fix?
options: Set deadlock_timeout to 0 so deadlocks are detected instantly
Switch every batch to a single-row INSERT with autocommit
Run the batches under SERIALIZABLE isolation
Sort each batch by the conflict key before upserting, and retry on 40P01
dbms-concurrency-recovery:1.explanation: Overlapping batches lock the same keys in different orders, which creates cycles. Sorting gives every worker the same lock order; a small retry handles anything left. Instant detection still aborts transactions, and single-row autocommit gives up batch atomicity and throughput.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:1.prompt: Compared with deadlock detection, what is the main downside of prevention schemes such as wait-die and wound-wait?
options: They may abort transactions even when no deadlock would have formed
They allow cycles in the wait-for graph
They require holding all locks until commit
They work only for read-only transactions
dbms-concurrency-recovery:1.explanation: Prevention aborts based on timestamp order whenever a conflict could lead to a cycle, so many of those aborts are unnecessary. Detection only aborts when a real cycle exists, at the cost of maintaining the graph.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:1.prompt: Which conditions must ALL hold at the same time for a deadlock to be possible (the Coffman conditions)? Select all that apply.
options: Mutual exclusion
Hold and wait
No preemption
Circular wait
Starvation
Priority inversion
dbms-concurrency-recovery:1.explanation: A deadlock needs exclusive resources, processes holding some while waiting for others, no forcible preemption, and a circular chain of waits. Starvation and priority inversion are separate liveness problems.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:1.prompt: Which are valid ways for a database or application to deal with lock deadlocks? Select all that apply.
options: A lock wait timeout (for example PostgreSQL lock_timeout) that aborts long waiters
Wait-for graph detection that aborts a victim
Acquiring locks in a consistent global order
Increasing the application's connection pool size
Raising every transaction to SERIALIZABLE isolation
dbms-concurrency-recovery:1.explanation: Timeouts break deadlocks crudely, detection breaks them precisely, and ordered acquisition prevents them. A bigger pool only allows more concurrent lock holders, and SERIALIZABLE adds serialization failures without stopping lock cycles.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:1.prompt: In PostgreSQL, the deadlock detector runs continuously, so a deadlock is broken the instant the cycle forms.
options: True
False
dbms-concurrency-recovery:1.explanation: PostgreSQL only runs the (fairly expensive) deadlock check after a lock wait exceeds deadlock_timeout, which defaults to 1s. Deadlocked transactions therefore sit blocked for about that long before one is aborted.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:2.prompt: In timestamp-ordering (TO) concurrency control, what decides the equivalent serial order of transactions?
options: The order in which they commit
The order in which they acquire their first lock
The timestamps they are assigned when they start
The number of items each one reads
dbms-concurrency-recovery:2.explanation: TO assigns each transaction a timestamp at start, and the schedule must equal the serial schedule in timestamp order. Commit order defines the order under rigorous 2PL, and TO doesn't use locks at all.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:2.prompt: Under basic timestamp ordering, T (TS=10) wants to read item X whose write timestamp W-TS(X) is 15. What happens?
options: T reads X and R-TS(X) becomes 15
T waits until the writer with TS=15 commits
T reads the older version of X
T is aborted and restarted with a new timestamp
dbms-concurrency-recovery:2.explanation: A younger transaction (TS=15) already overwrote X, so T would read a value that is 'from its future'. Basic TO rejects the read and restarts T. Reading an older version is what multiversion TO does; basic TO keeps only one version.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:2.prompt: Under basic timestamp ordering, T (TS=10) wants to write X. R-TS(X)=12 and W-TS(X)=8. What happens?
options: T is aborted, because a younger transaction already read the old value of X
The write succeeds and W-TS(X) becomes 10
The write is skipped under the Thomas write rule
T waits for the reader with TS=12 to finish
dbms-concurrency-recovery:2.explanation: The reader with TS=12 should have seen T's write if the order matched timestamps, but it already read the old value, so T must abort. The Thomas write rule only lets a write be skipped when W-TS > TS(T); here the conflict is with a read.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:2.prompt: With the Thomas write rule, T (TS=10) writes X where R-TS(X)=5 and W-TS(X)=12. What happens?
options: T is aborted, as in basic TO
The write overwrites X and W-TS(X) becomes 10
The write is ignored as obsolete and T continues
T waits for the transaction with TS=12 to commit
dbms-concurrency-recovery:2.explanation: A younger transaction (TS=12) already wrote X and nobody newer read T's slot, so in timestamp order T's write would be overwritten anyway. Skipping it is safe and gives view-serializable (not necessarily conflict-serializable) schedules. Basic TO would abort T.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:2.prompt: Why is basic timestamp ordering free of deadlocks?
options: It acquires all locks at transaction start
Transactions never wait for each other: conflicts cause immediate aborts
It uses a wait-for graph and aborts cycles
Only one transaction runs at a time
dbms-concurrency-recovery:2.explanation: When a conflict breaks timestamp order, basic TO aborts the offender instead of making it wait, so no waits-for cycle can form. The trade-off is more restarts and possible starvation of long transactions.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:2.prompt: What problem does basic timestamp ordering have that strict TO fixes by delaying reads and writes of items written by uncommitted transactions?
options: Deadlocks between readers and writers
Write skew between disjoint rows
Phantom rows in range queries
Unrecoverable schedules and cascading aborts from reading uncommitted values
dbms-concurrency-recovery:2.explanation: Basic TO lets T read X right after an uncommitted younger writer wrote it; if that writer aborts, T has read dirty data. Strict TO makes T wait until the writer commits or aborts. Waiting for older transactions only can't form a cycle, so it doesn't introduce deadlocks.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:2.prompt: A system uses basic TO. A long reporting transaction reads many hot rows that short transactions update constantly. What is the most likely result?
options: The report repeatedly finds rows with W-TS newer than its own timestamp and keeps being aborted
The report blocks all short transactions until it finishes
The short transactions deadlock with the report
The report sees a mix of old and new values but commits
dbms-concurrency-recovery:2.explanation: The long transaction's timestamp is old, so any row a younger transaction has updated is unreadable to it and it restarts. It can starve. TO never blocks writers or deadlocks, which rules out the second and third options.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:2.prompt: Under multiversion timestamp ordering (MVTO), T (TS=20) reads item X, which has versions written at TS 5, 15 and 25. Which version does T read?
options: The version written at TS 25, the newest
The version written at TS 15
The version written at TS 5, the oldest
None: T is aborted because a newer version exists
dbms-concurrency-recovery:2.explanation: MVTO gives T the version with the largest write timestamp ≤ TS(T), which is 15. That's why reads are never rejected in MVTO. Aborting on a newer write is basic single-version TO behaviour.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:2.prompt: Which statements about basic timestamp ordering are true? Select all that apply.
options: It is deadlock-free
Each data item tracks a read timestamp and a write timestamp
It guarantees conflict-serializable schedules
A transaction waits for older transactions to commit before reading
The Thomas write rule increases the number of aborts
dbms-concurrency-recovery:2.explanation: Basic TO keeps R-TS/W-TS per item, aborts instead of waiting (so no deadlocks), and enforces timestamp order (so schedules are conflict-serializable). Waiting is a feature of strict TO, and the Thomas write rule reduces aborts by skipping obsolete writes.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:2.prompt: Under basic timestamp ordering WITHOUT the Thomas write rule, which operations by T (TS=20) cause T to abort? Select all that apply.
options: Read X where W-TS(X)=25
Read X where W-TS(X)=10 and R-TS(X)=30
Write X where R-TS(X)=22
Write X where W-TS(X)=21 and R-TS(X)=5
Write X where R-TS(X)=18 and W-TS(X)=15
dbms-concurrency-recovery:2.explanation: Reads abort if W-TS > TS. Writes abort if R-TS > TS or W-TS > TS. A read is fine when only R-TS is newer (readers don't conflict), and a write with R-TS=18 and W-TS=15 (both < 20) succeeds.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:2.prompt: In timestamp-ordering concurrency control, a transaction's timestamp is assigned when it commits.
options: True
False
dbms-concurrency-recovery:2.explanation: TO assigns timestamps at transaction start, and every conflict check compares that start timestamp with item timestamps. Commit-time ordering is how optimistic validation or rigorous 2PL order transactions.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:3.prompt: In PostgreSQL, what physically happens when you UPDATE a row?
options: The row is modified in place and the old value is written to an undo log
A new tuple version is written, and the old one is marked with the updating transaction's id in xmax and stays until vacuumed
The old row is deleted immediately and its space is returned to the OS
The page is copied and the old page is discarded at commit
dbms-concurrency-recovery:3.explanation: PostgreSQL's MVCC writes a new tuple version and leaves the old one in the heap as a dead tuple once no snapshot needs it; VACUUM reclaims it later. In-place updates with an undo log are how Oracle and MySQL InnoDB work.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:3.prompt: What is the main concurrency benefit of MVCC in PostgreSQL?
options: Readers don't block writers and writers don't block readers
Two writers can update the same row at the same time
It removes the need for any locks
It makes every transaction serializable by default
dbms-concurrency-recovery:3.explanation: Readers see a snapshot of committed versions, so they never wait on row locks and never block writers. Concurrent writers to the same row still serialize on row locks, and the default isolation level is READ COMMITTED, not SERIALIZABLE.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:3.prompt: A PostgreSQL table keeps growing even though autovacuum runs often. pg_stat_activity shows a session that has been 'idle in transaction' for six hours. What is the most likely cause?
options: autovacuum_naptime is too short
The idle session holds an exclusive lock that stops autovacuum from starting
The table needs a REINDEX
The old transaction's snapshot holds back the xmin horizon, so VACUUM can't remove dead tuples newer than it
dbms-concurrency-recovery:3.explanation: VACUUM can only remove versions that no running transaction could still see. An open transaction pins the horizon, so dead tuples pile up. An idle transaction doesn't block VACUUM with a lock; it just makes dead tuples not yet removable.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:3.prompt: In PostgreSQL, how does plain VACUUM differ from VACUUM FULL?
options: Plain VACUUM rewrites the table; VACUUM FULL only updates statistics
Plain VACUUM takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock; VACUUM FULL runs online
Plain VACUUM marks dead space reusable without blocking reads or writes; VACUUM FULL rewrites the table into new files under an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock
They are aliases for the same operation
dbms-concurrency-recovery:3.explanation: Plain VACUUM makes space reusable within the table (returning only trailing empty pages to the OS) and runs alongside normal traffic. VACUUM FULL compacts the table and returns space to the OS, but blocks all access while it runs. The second option reverses them.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:3.prompt: Why must PostgreSQL eventually VACUUM even an insert-only table that never has dead tuples?
options: To freeze old tuples so that 32-bit transaction id wraparound can't make them look like they're in the future
To rebuild the table's indexes
To update the visibility of uncommitted inserts
To release disk space used by the inserts
dbms-concurrency-recovery:3.explanation: Transaction ids are 32-bit and wrap around. Old tuples must be frozen so they stay visible; if freezing falls too far behind, PostgreSQL stops assigning new xids to protect data. Insert-only tables have no dead tuples to reclaim, so freezing is the reason.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:3.prompt: A PostgreSQL table gets frequent updates to a non-indexed status column. Which change most helps these updates avoid writing new index entries?
options: Add an index on status
Lower the table's fillfactor so pages have free space for HOT (heap-only tuple) updates
Switch the column to JSONB
Run VACUUM FULL nightly
dbms-concurrency-recovery:3.explanation: HOT updates put the new version on the same page and skip index maintenance, but only when no indexed column changes and the page has room. A lower fillfactor leaves that room. Indexing status would make HOT impossible for those updates.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:3.prompt: In PostgreSQL under REPEATABLE READ, T1 and T2 both read row R. T1 updates R and commits. T2 then tries to update R. What happens?
options: T2's update applies to the new version of R, as under READ COMMITTED
T2's update silently overwrites T1's change
T2 gets 'could not serialize access due to concurrent update' and must retry the transaction
T2 blocks forever until T1's snapshot is vacuumed
dbms-concurrency-recovery:3.explanation: Under REPEATABLE READ, T2 can't modify a row changed by a transaction that committed after T2's snapshot was taken, so PostgreSQL raises a serialization failure (40001). Re-evaluating against the new version is READ COMMITTED behaviour.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:3.prompt: Which hidden system columns does PostgreSQL use to decide whether a tuple version is visible to a snapshot?
options: ctid and oid
xmin (inserting transaction) and xmax (deleting or locking transaction)
tableoid and cmin
lsn and checksum
dbms-concurrency-recovery:3.explanation: A version is visible if its xmin committed before the snapshot and its xmax is empty, aborted, or not yet committed as of the snapshot. ctid is the physical location and doesn't decide visibility.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:3.prompt: In PostgreSQL, which of these can cause dead tuples to accumulate faster than autovacuum can remove them? Select all that apply.
options: Frequent UPDATEs to the same rows
A session left 'idle in transaction' for hours
A forgotten prepared transaction (PREPARE TRANSACTION never committed or rolled back)
Read-only SELECTs that each finish in milliseconds
Adding a B-tree index to the table
dbms-concurrency-recovery:3.explanation: Updates create dead versions, and long-open or orphaned prepared transactions hold back the xmin horizon so those versions can't be removed. Short SELECTs release their snapshot quickly, and an extra index adds index size, not dead heap tuples.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:3.prompt: Which statements about snapshots in PostgreSQL are true? Select all that apply.
options: READ COMMITTED takes a new snapshot for each statement
REPEATABLE READ uses one snapshot taken at the transaction's first statement
PostgreSQL's REPEATABLE READ does not allow phantom reads
REPEATABLE READ prevents write skew between transactions that update different rows
dbms-concurrency-recovery:3.explanation: REPEATABLE READ in PostgreSQL is snapshot isolation, so re-running a query returns the same rows (no phantoms). It still allows write skew, where two transactions each read overlapping data and update different rows; only SERIALIZABLE (SSI) catches that.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:3.prompt: In PostgreSQL, a DELETE immediately frees the deleted row's space so new inserts can reuse it.
options: True
False
dbms-concurrency-recovery:3.explanation: DELETE only sets xmax on the tuple. Other snapshots may still need it, so the space is reclaimed only once VACUUM finds the tuple dead to every transaction.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:4.prompt: Users edit a product description in a form for several minutes before saving. Concurrent edits of the same product are rare. Which concurrency approach fits best?
options: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE when the form opens, held until save
A table-level lock while any form is open
Optimistic locking: store a version, and reject the save if the version changed
No control: the last save wins
dbms-concurrency-recovery:4.explanation: Optimistic locking holds nothing during user think time and catches the rare conflict at save time. Holding a row lock across an HTTP round-trip and minutes of editing ties up connections and blocks others; last-write-wins silently loses edits.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:4.prompt: In PostgreSQL, what does SELECT ... FROM accounts WHERE id = 1 FOR UPDATE do inside a transaction?
options: Locks the row until the transaction ends, so other FOR UPDATE, UPDATE or DELETE on it wait
Locks the whole accounts table until the transaction ends
Reads the latest committed row and releases the lock after the statement
Blocks all other SELECTs on the row
dbms-concurrency-recovery:4.explanation: FOR UPDATE takes a row-level lock held to commit or rollback. Competing writers and lockers wait, but plain SELECTs still read the last committed version via MVCC. It doesn't lock the table.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:4.prompt: Your code runs this, and the driver reports rowCount = 0. What does that mean, and what should the code do?
options: The row was locked; wait and run the same statement again
Another writer changed the row since it was read; reload it and retry or report a conflict
The UPDATE succeeded but the driver didn't count it
The account doesn't exist, so insert it
dbms-concurrency-recovery:4.explanation: Zero rows means the version in the WHERE clause no longer matches, so someone else committed a change. The safe response is to re-read and re-apply the change or surface a 409. Re-running the same statement will keep matching zero rows.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:4.prompt: Several Node workers pull jobs from a PostgreSQL jobs table. Which query lets each worker claim different pending jobs without blocking on rows another worker has already claimed?
options: SELECT ... WHERE status='pending' LIMIT 10 FOR UPDATE NOWAIT
SELECT ... WHERE status='pending' LIMIT 10 FOR SHARE
SELECT ... WHERE status='pending' LIMIT 10 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
SELECT ... WHERE status='pending' LIMIT 10 (no lock)
dbms-concurrency-recovery:4.explanation: SKIP LOCKED passes over rows other workers have locked, so each worker gets its own batch. NOWAIT throws an error as soon as it hits a locked row; FOR SHARE allows two workers to share-lock the same job; no lock lets workers grab the same rows.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:4.prompt: This Node code (node-postgres Pool) is meant to stop two requests withdrawing from the same account at once. Why doesn't the lock protect anything?
options: FOR UPDATE doesn't work with parameterized queries
Each pool.query runs in its own autocommit transaction, possibly on a different connection, so the lock is released as soon as the SELECT finishes
node-postgres strips FOR UPDATE clauses
The UPDATE needs FOR UPDATE as well
dbms-concurrency-recovery:4.explanation: Row locks last until the transaction ends, and without BEGIN each statement is its own transaction. Use one client from pool.connect(), then BEGIN, SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, UPDATE, COMMIT, and release the client.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:4.prompt: Two requests both read balance = 100 and each writes back balance = 100 - 30, so one withdrawal is lost. Which fix needs neither explicit locks nor a version column?
options: Use one atomic statement: UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 30 WHERE id = $1 AND balance >= 30
Read the balance twice before writing
Wrap the read and the write in a READ COMMITTED transaction
Cache the balance in Redis
dbms-concurrency-recovery:4.explanation: A single UPDATE that computes from the current value does the read and write under the row lock, so concurrent withdrawals serialize, and the guard prevents overdraft. Read-then-write inside READ COMMITTED still loses updates, because the plain SELECT takes no lock.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:4.prompt: A flash-sale counter row is updated by thousands of concurrent requests using optimistic locking (read version, then update WHERE version = ?). What is the most likely outcome?
options: Throughput rises, because no locks are held
Most attempts fail the version check and retry, so throughput collapses under contention
Deadlocks become frequent
Updates are lost silently
dbms-concurrency-recovery:4.explanation: Optimistic locking assumes conflicts are rare. On one hot row nearly every attempt conflicts and retries, wasting work. An atomic UPDATE ... SET n = n - 1 (or a pessimistic lock) serializes cheaply. Updates aren't lost: version checks catch conflicts.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:4.prompt: An admin endpoint should fail immediately with an error if the target row is already locked, rather than waiting. Which PostgreSQL clause fits?
options: FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
FOR UPDATE NOWAIT
FOR KEY SHARE
SET lock_timeout = 0
dbms-concurrency-recovery:4.explanation: NOWAIT raises an error at once if any target row is locked. SKIP LOCKED silently leaves the row out of the result, which hides the conflict. lock_timeout = 0 disables the timeout, meaning wait forever.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:4.prompt: Which are genuine advantages of optimistic locking over pessimistic locking? Select all that apply.
options: No database locks are held during user think time
Works naturally across stateless HTTP requests, for example with ETag and If-Match
Reading for an edit never blocks on another editor's row lock
Guarantees that no request ever has to retry
Performs best when many writers update the same row
dbms-concurrency-recovery:4.explanation: Optimistic locking checks the version at write time, so nothing is held between requests and it maps well to HTTP conditional requests. The price is retries on conflict, which makes it a poor fit for heavily contended rows.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:4.prompt: Which of these correctly implement optimistic concurrency control? Select all that apply.
options: UPDATE ... WHERE id = ? AND version = ?, treating 0 affected rows as a conflict
Clients send If-Match with the resource's ETag, and the server answers 412 if it changed
MongoDB updateOne({ _id, version }, { $set: {...}, $inc: { version: 1 } }), checking matchedCount
Read the row, compare its version in application code, then UPDATE ... WHERE id = ? without the version
dbms-concurrency-recovery:4.explanation: The version check has to happen atomically with the write. Each correct option puts the condition in the write itself. Checking in app code and then updating leaves a gap where another writer can commit.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:4.prompt: In PostgreSQL, a plain SELECT (no FOR UPDATE or FOR SHARE) waits if another transaction holds a FOR UPDATE lock on the row.
options: True
False
dbms-concurrency-recovery:4.explanation: Plain SELECTs read a snapshot of committed versions and ignore row locks. Only writers and other locking reads (FOR UPDATE, FOR SHARE, and so on) wait.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:5.prompt: What does the write-ahead logging (WAL) rule require?
options: Data pages must be written to disk before their log records
Log records describing a change must reach stable storage before the modified data page is written, and the commit record must be flushed before commit is acknowledged
Every transaction writes its log and data pages in one fsync
The log is written only at checkpoints
dbms-concurrency-recovery:5.explanation: Logging first means any change on disk can be undone or redone from the log, and a commit is durable once its commit record is flushed, even if data pages aren't. Data-before-log is the reverse and breaks recovery.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:5.prompt: Why does WAL let a database acknowledge commits faster than writing changed data pages at commit time?
options: The WAL is kept only in memory
WAL writes are sequential appends, while data page writes would be random I/O across many pages
WAL skips fsync entirely
WAL compresses data pages
dbms-concurrency-recovery:5.explanation: A commit only needs a sequential flush of the log tail. Dirty pages can be written lazily later. The WAL is still fsynced (unless you relax that), so durability isn't given up.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:5.prompt: What is the main purpose of a checkpoint in a WAL-based database such as PostgreSQL?
options: To make committed transactions durable
To flush dirty pages so crash recovery can start replaying from the checkpoint's redo point, bounding recovery time and letting older WAL be recycled
To take a consistent backup
To vacuum dead tuples
dbms-concurrency-recovery:5.explanation: Recovery has to replay WAL from the last checkpoint's redo point, so checkpoints limit how much needs replaying, and WAL before that point can be removed (unless replicas or archiving still need it). Durability comes from flushing commit records, not from checkpoints.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:5.prompt: In what order does ARIES run its recovery phases after a crash?
options: Redo, Undo, Analysis
Undo, Redo, Analysis
Analysis, Redo, Undo
Analysis, Undo, Redo
dbms-concurrency-recovery:5.explanation: Analysis rebuilds the dirty page and active transaction tables from the last checkpoint, Redo repeats history to restore the state at the crash, and Undo rolls back transactions that never committed.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:5.prompt: During its redo phase, ARIES reapplies updates from ALL transactions, including those that will be rolled back. Why?
options: To find out which transactions committed
Because undo can't run without a checkpoint
To restore the exact database state at the crash so that undo, driven by LSNs and log records, can correctly roll back the losers
To compress the log
dbms-concurrency-recovery:5.explanation: This 'repeating history' makes page state match the log, so undo can safely reverse loser updates, including partial rollbacks already in the log. Analysis, not redo, determines which transactions committed.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:5.prompt: What role do compensation log records (CLRs) play in ARIES?
options: They record each undo action, are redo-only, and point to the next record to undo, so a crash during recovery never undoes the same change twice
They store checksums for torn-page detection
They mark the start of a checkpoint
They log index splits for replication
dbms-concurrency-recovery:5.explanation: Each undo writes a CLR whose UndoNextLSN skips past what has already been undone. If recovery crashes and restarts, redo replays the CLRs and undo continues from where it stopped, which bounds the work and avoids double undo.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:5.prompt: A buffer manager may write uncommitted dirty pages to disk (steal) and doesn't force committed pages to disk at commit (no-force). What must recovery support?
options: Only redo
Only undo
Neither, because the log is enough
Both undo (for stolen uncommitted changes) and redo (for committed changes not yet on disk)
dbms-concurrency-recovery:5.explanation: Steal puts loser changes on disk, which need undo. No-force can leave winner changes missing from disk, which need redo. ARIES is designed for steal/no-force because it gives the buffer manager the most freedom.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:5.prompt: In PostgreSQL, a team sets synchronous_commit = off for a high-volume event table. What risk are they accepting?
options: Table corruption after a crash
A crash can lose the most recent commits that were acknowledged but not yet flushed to WAL, while the database stays consistent
Replicas will diverge permanently
Transactions may see uncommitted data
dbms-concurrency-recovery:5.explanation: With synchronous_commit off, COMMIT returns before the WAL flush. A crash may lose a short window of transactions (up to about three times wal_writer_delay), but WAL ordering keeps the database consistent. It doesn't change isolation.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:5.prompt: Which statements about checkpoints in PostgreSQL are true? Select all that apply.
options: More frequent checkpoints shorten crash recovery
More frequent checkpoints increase write I/O, partly because of more full-page writes after each checkpoint
WAL before the latest checkpoint's redo point can be recycled unless replication or archiving still needs it
A transaction becomes durable only when the next checkpoint completes
dbms-concurrency-recovery:5.explanation: Checkpoint frequency trades recovery time against I/O: the first change to each page after a checkpoint logs a full page image. Durability comes from the commit record's WAL flush, not from checkpoints.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:5.prompt: Which features in PostgreSQL are built on the write-ahead log? Select all that apply.
options: Crash recovery
Streaming physical replication
Point-in-time recovery from a base backup plus archived WAL
Logical decoding for change data capture
Query plan caching
Deciding row visibility for MVCC snapshots
dbms-concurrency-recovery:5.explanation: The WAL is replayed for recovery, shipped to standbys, archived for PITR, and decoded for logical replication and CDC. Plan caching is per session, and visibility is decided from tuple xmin/xmax plus the commit log, not by reading WAL.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:5.prompt: In ARIES redo, a logged update is reapplied to a page only if the page's pageLSN is lower than the log record's LSN.
options: True
False
dbms-concurrency-recovery:5.explanation: pageLSN records the last update applied to the page. If it's already ≥ the record's LSN, the change is on disk and redo skips it. That makes redo idempotent.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:6.prompt: Why do teams put a pooler like PgBouncer in front of PostgreSQL when they run many app instances?
options: PostgreSQL forks a backend process per connection, so thousands of client connections waste memory and hit max_connections
PostgreSQL caps clients at 10 connections
PgBouncer caches query results
PgBouncer shards writes across replicas
dbms-concurrency-recovery:6.explanation: Each PostgreSQL connection is a separate process with its own memory and setup cost, so many mostly-idle connections are expensive. PgBouncer multiplexes clients onto a small server pool. It doesn't cache results or shard.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:6.prompt: In PgBouncer transaction pooling mode, when is a server connection assigned to a client?
options: For the client's whole session
For a single statement only
For the duration of one transaction, then returned to the pool
Only for write statements
dbms-concurrency-recovery:6.explanation: In transaction mode the client gets a server connection from BEGIN (or an implicit single-statement transaction) until COMMIT or ROLLBACK. Session mode pins the connection for the whole session; statement mode releases it after every statement.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:6.prompt: Behind PgBouncer in transaction mode, which of these behaves correctly?
options: SET search_path = tenant_a, run once after connecting
LISTEN orders_channel, to receive notifications later
SELECT pg_advisory_lock(42), released at the end of the request
SET LOCAL statement_timeout = '2s' inside a BEGIN ... COMMIT block
dbms-concurrency-recovery:6.explanation: SET LOCAL lasts only for the current transaction, which is exactly the unit PgBouncer pins. A session-level SET, LISTEN or session advisory lock stays on whichever server connection you used, which may then go to a different client.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:6.prompt: 20 Node instances each create a node-postgres Pool with max: 20 against a PostgreSQL server with max_connections = 100. What happens at peak, and what is a sound fix?
options: Up to 400 connections are attempted and many fail; add PgBouncer in transaction mode and/or shrink per-instance pools so the total fits
Node shares one pool across instances automatically
PostgreSQL queues the extra 300 connections internally
Raise max_connections to 10000
dbms-concurrency-recovery:6.explanation: Pools are per process, so the total demand is instances × max. PostgreSQL rejects connections beyond max_connections ('too many clients'). A shared pooler or smaller pools keep the backend count sane; a huge max_connections wastes memory and adds contention.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:6.prompt: On an 8-core PostgreSQL server, a team raises the pooler's server pool from 50 to 500 connections, expecting more throughput. What usually happens?
options: Throughput rises roughly 10x
Throughput stays flat or drops, because extra active backends add context switching and lock contention without more CPU or disk
Queries become serializable
PgBouncer refuses pools larger than the core count
dbms-concurrency-recovery:6.explanation: Throughput peaks with a fairly small number of active connections, on the order of a few times the core count depending on I/O. Past that point, queuing in the pooler beats contention inside the database.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:6.prompt: A Node service checks out a client with `const client = await pool.connect()` but forgets client.release() on an error path. What symptom appears over time?
options: Queries return stale data
PostgreSQL kills the connections at once
The pool runs out of clients, and new requests hang waiting for a connection
The pool silently opens unlimited extra connections
dbms-concurrency-recovery:6.explanation: Clients that are never released stay checked out forever. Once all max clients have leaked, pool.connect() and pool.query() wait, indefinitely by default unless connectionTimeoutMillis is set. Use try/finally to always release.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:6.prompt: A handler runs BEGIN, updates an order, calls a payment provider over HTTP (2-5 seconds), then COMMITs. Behind PgBouncer in transaction mode, pool waits climb under load. What is the best fix?
options: Switch PgBouncer to session mode
Raise default_pool_size until waits stop
Disable transactions for this handler
Move the HTTP call outside the transaction and keep transactions short
dbms-concurrency-recovery:6.explanation: The server connection is pinned for the whole transaction, including the slow network call, so a few requests starve the pool and also hold row locks. Session mode pins even longer, and a bigger pool just pushes contention into the database.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:6.prompt: Which PgBouncer pooling mode does not allow multi-statement transactions at all?
options: Session
Transaction
Statement
Replication
dbms-concurrency-recovery:6.explanation: Statement mode returns the server connection after every statement, so a multi-statement transaction would span connections. PgBouncer therefore refuses them. Transaction mode supports them by pinning for the whole transaction.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:6.prompt: Why is PgBouncer transaction pooling attractive for a serverless Node app on PostgreSQL? Select all that apply.
options: Many short-lived function instances each open connections
It keeps the number of PostgreSQL backend processes small
Client connections to PgBouncer are cheap compared with PostgreSQL backends
It makes session-level advisory locks safe across invocations
It makes each individual query execute faster on the server
dbms-concurrency-recovery:6.explanation: Serverless scales to many instances, and the pooler absorbs their connections and multiplexes them onto a small pool of backends. It doesn't make session state safe (it breaks it) and doesn't speed up execution itself.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:6.prompt: Which features break or misbehave behind PgBouncer in transaction pooling mode? Select all that apply.
options: Session-level SET (without LOCAL)
A long-lived LISTEN for NOTIFY events
Session-level advisory locks (pg_advisory_lock)
Temporary tables expected to survive across transactions
SET LOCAL inside a transaction
Several statements inside one BEGIN ... COMMIT
dbms-concurrency-recovery:6.explanation: Anything stored on the server session leaks to, or disappears for, other clients when the connection is reassigned after a transaction. SET LOCAL and statements within a single transaction stay on one pinned connection, so they're fine.

dbms-concurrency-recovery:6.prompt: PgBouncer in transaction mode lets many client connections share a much smaller number of PostgreSQL server connections.
options: True
False
dbms-concurrency-recovery:6.explanation: That's its main purpose. Because clients only hold a server connection during a transaction, thousands of mostly-idle clients can share tens of backends.
